questions.stem: A 58-year-old client from a close-knit religious family must decide whether to have a second open-heart surgery. The family gathers to pray and talk with their pastor before each treatment decision. A newly hired nurse says, “They’re just stalling. That’s the wrong way to decide.” Which response by the precepting nurse best reflects an understanding of moral development?
options: “Capable clients have the right to decide, so we respect their choice.”
“Let’s offer chaplain support to the family while they pray and decide.”
“Their faith, family, and life experiences shape how they decide. We support that.”
“Let’s make sure the family has accurate facts about the surgery risks.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Respecting autonomy is true and important, but it does not explain why this family decides the way it does or correct the new nurse’s judgment about moral development.
Incorrect. Offering spiritual support is a kind action, but it does not address the new nurse’s view that the family’s process is wrong.
Correct. This response teaches that moral development is shaped by faith, family, culture, and life experience, and that the nurse supports the family’s own decision process rather than judging it.
Incorrect. Making sure the client has accurate information is part of the nurse’s role, but it is incomplete; it does not address respect for the family’s moral perspective.
questions.rationale: Moral development is the process of learning right from wrong. It is shaped by family, culture, religion, education, and life experiences, and it guides how clients and families make health care decisions. Prayer and talking with a pastor are part of this family’s moral process, not stalling. The best response teaches the new nurse to respect that process. Affirming autonomy, offering chaplain support, or checking that the family has accurate facts are all reasonable, but none corrects the new nurse’s judgment about how this family makes moral decisions.
questions.takeaway: Clients’ moral views come from family, culture, religion, education, and experience; support their way of deciding instead of judging it.
questions.hintContent: Think about where a person’s sense of right and wrong comes from and whose decision this is.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that judge, pressure, or steer the client; choose the one that respects the client’s moral perspective.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing for a care conference with a 34-year-old client who must decide whether to join a clinical trial of an experimental treatment. To understand the client’s moral perspective on the decision, which areas should the nurse explore? Select all that apply.
options: The family values and upbringing that shaped the client
The client’s cultural background and its views on illness
The client’s religious or spiritual beliefs about treatment
Past life experiences, such as a parent’s death in an ICU
The choice most clients on this unit usually make
The nurse’s own view of what the right choice would be
optionRationales: Correct. Family is a primary influence on moral development and shapes how the client weighs choices.
Correct. Culture shapes moral development; morals vary by culture (cultural relativism).
Correct. Religion is one of the main influences on a person’s moral development.
Correct. Life experiences shape moral development and often drive treatment decisions.
Incorrect. What other clients choose says nothing about this client’s own moral perspective.
Incorrect. The nurse’s own view is not part of the client’s moral perspective and could steer the decision.
questions.rationale: Moral development, the process of learning right from wrong, is influenced by family, culture, religion, education, and life experiences. Exploring these areas helps the nurse understand the client’s moral perspective, which shapes health care decisions. Considering culture during assessment reflects cultural relativism: morals vary by culture. What other clients choose and the nurse’s personal opinion are not sources of this client’s values; relying on them risks steering the client.
questions.takeaway: Assess family, culture, religion, education, and life experiences to understand a client’s moral perspective.
questions.hintContent: Recall the influences on moral development listed in your course.
questions.hintStrategy: Select only the factors that come from the client’s own life; reject anything that substitutes someone else’s view.

questions.stem: A nurse is admitting a 70-year-old client who immigrated from a culture in which the eldest son makes medical decisions for the family. The client speaks some English. Her son answers every assessment question for her and says he will sign her consent forms. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask the client privately, through an interpreter, how she wants decisions made.
Direct the questions to the son, as is customary in the client’s culture.
Ask the son to interpret so his mother understands each question asked.
Request an ethics consult about who should make the client’s decisions.
optionRationales: Correct. Asking the client privately, with a professional interpreter, confirms her own wishes. A capable adult may choose to let her son decide, but the nurse must hear that choice from her first.
Incorrect. Respecting cultural customs matters, but the nurse cannot assume the client’s preference. The son has no legal authority until she chooses to give it.
Incorrect. Including family is reasonable, but family members should not interpret. A professional interpreter ensures accurate, unbiased communication.
Incorrect. An ethics consult may help if a conflict develops, but it is premature. The nurse first asks the client directly how she wants decisions made.
questions.rationale: During assessment, the nurse considers cultural relativism: morals vary by culture, and family-centered decision making may be right within this client’s culture. Autonomy still belongs to the client. A capable adult may choose to let a family member speak or decide, but the nurse must confirm that choice with the client directly and privately, using a professional interpreter rather than the son. Deferring to the son without asking her, using him as interpreter, or jumping to an ethics consult all skip the step of hearing the client’s own wishes.
questions.takeaway: Respect cultural decision patterns, but confirm privately that the capable client chooses them.
questions.hintContent: Whose choice is it to involve the son, and how would the nurse know?
questions.hintStrategy: In culture-and-autonomy items, pick the answer that asks the client directly rather than judging or assuming.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old client with paraplegia after a car crash 3 months ago tells the nurse, “Nobody asks what I want anymore. My friends stopped visiting, and I’m alone all day. I still wake up with nightmares about the crash.” Which nursing diagnoses are supported by these data? Select all that apply.
options: Powerlessness
Social Isolation
Post-Trauma Syndrome
Acute Confusion
Deficient Knowledge
optionRationales: Correct. “Nobody asks what I want anymore” reflects a perceived lack of control over his situation.
Correct. Friends no longer visit and he is alone all day, which he experiences as unwanted.
Correct. Nightmares about the crash months later reflect an ongoing response to a traumatic event.
Incorrect. Nothing in the data suggests a sudden change in attention, orientation, or thinking.
Incorrect. The client does not show a lack of information about his condition or care.
questions.rationale: Your course lists nursing diagnoses related to moral issues: Moral Distress, Noncompliance, Social Isolation, Powerlessness, and Post-Trauma Syndrome. This client’s statements match three of them. Feeling that no one asks what he wants supports Powerlessness. Friends no longer visiting and being alone supports Social Isolation. Recurrent nightmares about the crash support Post-Trauma Syndrome. No cues suggest confusion or a knowledge gap.
questions.takeaway: Match each client statement to the diagnosis it supports; moral issues often show up as powerlessness, isolation, or trauma responses.
questions.hintContent: Link each quoted statement to one diagnosis.
questions.hintStrategy: For diagnosis SATA items, select only diagnoses with a clear cue in the stem.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old client with metastatic cancer and decision-making capacity decided to stop chemotherapy. Her adult children keep pressuring her to continue. She tells the nurse, “I know stopping is right for me, but I keep giving in to them, and it’s tearing me apart.” Which nursing diagnosis best fits these data?
options: Decisional Conflict
Moral Distress
Anxiety
Interrupted Family Processes
optionRationales: Incorrect. Decisional Conflict fits a person who is unsure which choice to make. This client is certain that stopping chemotherapy is right; her problem is being blocked from acting on it.
Correct. Moral Distress fits best: she knows the right action for herself but feels unable to carry it out because of family pressure, and she describes inner anguish.
Incorrect. She is clearly upset, but Anxiety is too general. It does not capture the core problem of knowing the right action and feeling blocked from it.
Incorrect. Family conflict is present, but the data center on her own anguish over not acting on her decision, which Moral Distress describes more precisely.
questions.rationale: Moral distress occurs when a person knows the right action but feels blocked from carrying it out. This client has decided that stopping chemotherapy is right for her, yet family pressure keeps her from acting on that decision, and she describes inner anguish. Moral Distress is one of the nursing diagnoses related to moral issues on your course slides. The nurse supports her autonomy, for example by arranging a family meeting with the provider so her choice can be heard.
questions.takeaway: Knowing the right choice but feeling unable to act on it is moral distress.
questions.hintContent: Look at the gap between what she believes is right and what she is doing.
questions.hintStrategy: Pick the diagnosis whose definition matches the client’s exact words.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old client with end-stage kidney disease and decision-making capacity has decided to stop dialysis and enter hospice. The nephrologist and several nurses believe he should continue. As the nurse revises the plan of care, which action is the priority?
options: Request a psychiatric consult to confirm his decision-making capacity.
Write comfort-focused goals and refer him to hospice services.
Notify the ethics committee to resolve the team’s disagreement.
Write goals around his wishes and set up a care conference with the team.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Assessing capacity matters when it is in doubt, but he already has capacity. Disagreeing with the team is not a sign of incapacity.
Incorrect. Comfort goals and hospice referral honor his wishes, but this is incomplete. It does not address the team’s differing values or open communication.
Incorrect. An ethics committee is an option if conflict cannot be resolved, but it is premature. A care conference is the first step toward shared understanding.
Correct. The plan reflects the client’s goals, and a care conference supports open communication and collaborative decision making among the client, family, and team.
questions.rationale: Your course notes that planning may be difficult when the client’s or family’s values differ from the health care team’s. A capable adult may refuse life-sustaining treatment, including dialysis. The nurse writes the plan around the client’s goals, such as comfort and hospice referral, and uses a care conference to support open communication and collaborative decision making among the client, family, and team. Questioning his capacity substitutes the team’s values for his, hospice referral alone leaves the team conflict unaddressed, and an ethics committee is a later step if the care conference does not resolve the disagreement.
questions.takeaway: When values differ, the plan of care follows the capable client’s goals.
questions.hintContent: Whose values should drive the goals in a capable client’s plan of care?
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the action that both honors the client’s decision and opens communication; reject delay and pressure.

questions.stem: Two days after a client died when his family chose to withdraw life support, a nurse tells her mentor, “I keep replaying that night. Did we do the right thing?” Which response by the mentor is most helpful?
options: “The family made a legal, ethical choice, and you cared for him well.”
“Second-guessing after a moral decision is common. Let’s talk it through.”
“Our employee assistance program offers free counseling for this.”
“Writing in a reflective journal can help you sort through it all.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reassurance is kind and likely true, but it closes the conversation instead of inviting the reflection that builds ethical skill.
Correct. This normalizes second-guessing after a moral decision and invites the nurse to debrief with an experienced peer, which reduces moral distress and burnout.
Incorrect. Counseling resources are appropriate if distress persists, but referring her out first misses the chance to debrief directly with her mentor.
Incorrect. Journaling supports self-reflection, but doing it alone is less helpful than talking it through with an experienced mentor.
questions.rationale: In the evaluation step of the nursing process, moral decisions often lead to second-guessing or self-reflection. That reflection is normal and can build ethical skill. Talking with a mentor or experienced peer, debriefing, and using support systems reduce moral distress and burnout. Quick reassurance, an immediate referral, or solo journaling can help, but each is less effective than talking it through with the mentor right now.
questions.takeaway: Second-guessing after a moral decision is normal; debrief with a mentor or peer.
questions.hintContent: Which step of the nursing process involves looking back on a decision?
questions.hintStrategy: For moral distress items, choose the response that validates and offers support.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client with decision-making capacity is dying of cardiogenic shock. He has a do-not-resuscitate order, and the care plan is comfort-focused. He rates his chest pain 9/10 and says, “Please give me something. I know I’m dying.” His blood pressure is 72/40 mm Hg and heart rate is 128/min. Morphine 2 mg IV every 15 minutes as needed for pain is prescribed. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the prescribed morphine slowly, then reassess his pain and comfort.
Hold the morphine because his blood pressure is too low for an opioid.
Give half of the prescribed dose so his blood pressure does not fall further.
Ask the family whether they agree with giving morphine before giving it.
optionRationales: Correct. Relieving a dying client’s severe pain with a prescribed opioid is ethical when the intent is comfort. This is the principle of double effect.
Incorrect. In comfort-focused care for a dying client, low blood pressure is not a reason to leave him in severe pain.
Incorrect. Changing the dose without a prescription is outside the nurse’s scope and leaves pain undertreated.
Incorrect. The client has capacity and has asked for relief; the decision is his, not his family’s.
questions.rationale: The client is dying, has capacity, has chosen comfort-focused care with a DNR order, and asks for pain relief. Under the principle of double effect, giving a prescribed opioid is ethical when the act is good, the intent is to relieve pain rather than cause death, death is not the means of relief, and the benefit outweighs the risk. The nurse gives the drug slowly and reassesses after the dose. Opioids titrated to relieve symptoms in dying clients have generally not been shown to shorten life. Withholding or cutting the dose leaves him suffering, and family consent is not needed for a capable client.
questions.takeaway: At the end of life, give prescribed pain medicine to relieve suffering; intent to comfort makes it ethical.
questions.hintContent: Consider the goals of care, who has the right to decide, and what the nurse intends.
questions.hintStrategy: In comfort-care items, choose the action that relieves suffering within the prescription; reject withholding based on vital signs alone.
questions.ref: Module 44 · Ethics · Morality (Exemplar 44.A) · Unit 7 slide 5; Verbatim Account handout
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

questions.stem: A hospice nurse is teaching a nursing student about giving opioids to relieve severe pain in dying clients. Which statements by the student show correct understanding of the principle of double effect? Select all that apply.
options: “The purpose of each dose must be to relieve pain, not to cause death.”
“The comfort the drug gives must outweigh the risk of its side effects.”
“An earlier death may be foreseen as possible, but it must not be intended.”
“Death must never be the way the client’s pain gets relieved.”
“If the client asks, I may give a large dose to end his suffering quickly.”
“I should hold the opioid if there is any chance it could lower blood pressure.”
optionRationales: Correct. Intent is central: the good effect (pain relief) must be the only one intended.
Correct. Proportionality: the good effect must outweigh the possible harm.
Correct. A bad effect may be foreseen but not intended.
Correct. The bad effect cannot be the means of achieving the good effect.
Incorrect. Giving a dose in order to cause death is euthanasia, which is illegal and against the nursing code.
Incorrect. A possible side effect does not justify leaving a dying client in severe pain when relief is the goal.
questions.rationale: The principle of double effect says an act with a good and a bad effect is ethical when the act itself is good, only the good effect is intended, the bad effect is not the means to the good effect, and the good outweighs the bad. This is the reasoning in the Verbatim Account, where the nurse gave morphine to end the client’s pain, not his life. Giving a large dose to end life is euthanasia. Withholding comfort medication for any possible risk violates beneficence for a dying client.
questions.takeaway: Double effect: good act, good intent, harm not the means, and benefit outweighs harm.
questions.hintContent: Think about intent, means, and proportion.
questions.hintStrategy: Reject statements that intend death or that let a remote risk block comfort.
questions.ref: Module 44 · Ethics · Morality (Exemplar 44.A) · Unit 7 slide 5; Verbatim Account handout

questions.stem: A nurse educator is preparing orientation examples of the principle “strive for the least harm possible.” Which nursing actions should the educator include as examples of this principle? Select all that apply.
options: Performing hand hygiene before and after every client contact
Checking a client’s allergy history before giving a new antibiotic
Monitoring a client on chemotherapy for side effects and reporting them early
Arranging transportation so a client can attend cardiac rehabilitation
Giving an uninsured client the same pain reassessments as other clients
Telling a client the truth about a medication error per the disclosure policy
optionRationales: Correct. Hand hygiene prevents health care–associated infections, a key nonmaleficence duty.
Correct. Checking allergies before medications is the course’s example of nonmaleficence.
Correct. Treatments like chemotherapy carry known harms; monitoring and early reporting keeps harm as small as possible.
Incorrect. This is a positive act to promote welfare, which is beneficence.
Incorrect. Equal care regardless of insurance reflects justice.
Incorrect. Telling the truth about a mistake reflects veracity.
questions.rationale: Nonmaleficence means doing no harm. Because health care sometimes causes unintended harm, such as health care–associated (nosocomial) infections, adverse drug reactions, and side effects of chemotherapy or radiation, nurses weigh risks and benefits and strive for the least harm possible. Hand hygiene, allergy checks, and monitoring for side effects all reduce harm. Arranging rehabilitation is beneficence, equal care regardless of insurance is justice, and truthful error disclosure is veracity.
questions.takeaway: Nonmaleficence: prevent and minimize harm, and never cause harm on purpose.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each action mainly prevents harm or does something else, like promoting good or fairness.
questions.hintStrategy: Translate each action into its purpose, then match the purpose to the principle.
questions.ref: Module 44 · Ethics · Ethical Principles · Unit 7 slide 5; Further Illustrations handout
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: A 59-year-old client with liver cirrhosis and decision-making capacity is being discharged. He tells the nurse, “I know what the doctor said, but I’m going to keep having a few beers at night.” Which response by the nurse respects his autonomy while still promoting his welfare?
options: “That is your choice to make as an adult, and I respect your decision.”
“Drinking will damage your liver even more, so you really need to stop.”
“Would you like to talk about your liver and get resources to help you cut back?”
“Let’s review the signs of liver problems you should report to your doctor.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This respects his autonomy, but it is incomplete. It does not promote his welfare with teaching or resources.
Incorrect. The statement is true and aims to help, but telling a capable adult what he must do is paternalistic and does not respect his autonomy.
Correct. This response accepts his choice while offering teaching and resources to reduce harm, balancing autonomy with beneficence.
Incorrect. Teaching warning signs promotes safety, but it ignores the drinking he just raised and misses the chance to offer help cutting back.
questions.rationale: Autonomy means respecting a capable client’s decisions even when they do not seem to be in his best interest, such as continuing to drink after a cirrhosis diagnosis. The unwanted outcome of beneficence is paternalism: deciding what is best and pressuring the client to act against his wishes, treating a capable adult like a child. The best response respects his choice while still offering accurate teaching and resources. Accepting his choice without offering help, telling him he must stop, or teaching around the drinking each meets only part of that goal.
questions.takeaway: Respect a capable client’s risky choice, and keep teaching and offering help without pressure.
questions.hintContent: Which option leaves the decision with the client but still offers something helpful?
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate answers that threaten, go around the client, or give up on him.
questions.ref: Module 44 · Ethics · Ethical Principles · Unit 7 slide 5; Further Illustrations handout

questions.stem: A hospital will offer free pediatric dental care to 45 children each month. About 120 families apply in the first month. Which method of selecting the children best reflects the principle of justice?
options: Accept the first 45 complete applications received each month.
Divide the openings equally among the areas the hospital serves.
Have a committee review each family’s story and choose freely.
Use need-based criteria applied the same way to every application.
optionRationales: Incorrect. First come, first served seems neutral, but it favors families with more time, access, and information rather than those with the greatest need.
Incorrect. Equal shares by area looks fair, but it ignores how need differs between areas and between children.
Incorrect. Committee review can be careful, but without set criteria applied the same way, personal bias can shape who is chosen.
Correct. Clear need-based criteria applied the same way to every application distribute a limited resource fairly and free from bias, which reflects justice.
questions.rationale: Justice is the equal right to goods regardless of what people contribute or who they are. When a resource is limited, such as 45 dental openings a month, justice requires a fair method that is free from bias to decide who receives it. Clear need-based criteria applied the same way to every family meet that standard; a lottery among eligible children would also be fair. First-come selection favors families with more access, equal shares by area ignore need, and case-by-case choice without set criteria invites bias.
questions.takeaway: Distribute scarce services with clear criteria applied equally to everyone.
questions.hintContent: Which option uses the same rule for every family?
questions.hintStrategy: For allocation items, choose consistent, unbiased criteria; reject favoritism and pressure.
questions.ref: Module 44 · Ethics · Ethical Principles · Unit 7 slide 5; Further Illustrations handout
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 4-year-old is crying before scheduled immunizations. His parent says, “Why hurt him with shots when he isn’t even sick?” Which response by the nurse best explains the ethical basis for the immunizations?
options: “Vaccines are very safe, and any side effects are usually mild and short.”
“The shots sting briefly, but they protect him and others from serious diseases.”
“School entry requires these shots by law, so he needs to get them today.”
“We can use numbing cream and distraction to ease his pain during them.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. This is true and reassuring, but it speaks to safety, not the ethical reason for causing brief pain in a well child.
Correct. This explains beneficence: the brief discomfort is outweighed by the benefit to the child and to others, which answers the parent’s question honestly.
Incorrect. School requirements are real, but a legal rule is not the ethical basis, and it does not explain why the benefit outweighs the harm.
Incorrect. Comfort measures are appropriate and should be used, but they do not explain why giving the shots is ethically justified.
questions.rationale: Your handout uses immunization as an example of beneficence: doing good for the client’s welfare even when the action carries some harm. The injection definitely causes brief discomfort, but the benefits to the child and to society outweigh it. The nurse explains this honestly, supports the parent’s informed decision, and uses comfort measures such as holding the child and distraction.
questions.takeaway: Beneficence can involve brief harm when the benefit clearly outweighs it.
questions.hintContent: Weigh the short-term discomfort against the long-term benefit.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the answer that honestly explains benefit versus harm; reject dismissive or blaming replies.
questions.ref: Module 44 · Ethics · Ethical Principles · Unit 7 slide 5; Further Illustrations handout

questions.stem: A 22-year-old client on a medical unit tells the nurse, “You’re the only one I trust. I’ve saved up pills at home, and I’m going to take them all once I’m discharged. Promise me you won’t tell anyone.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Explain to the client that the nurse cannot keep this plan a secret.
Document the statement and report it to the next shift during handoff.
Stay with the client and notify the provider and charge nurse right away.
Call the client’s parents and ask them to remove the pills from the home.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Being honest about limits of confidentiality is appropriate, but it is incomplete. It does not make the client safe or start suicide precautions.
Incorrect. Documenting and reporting are required, but waiting until handoff delays action on an immediate threat to life.
Correct. The client has a plan and means. Staying with the client and notifying the provider and charge nurse right away puts safety first and starts suicide precautions and full assessment.
Incorrect. Removing means at home is part of later safety planning, but it is not the first step and should be planned with the team and the client.
questions.rationale: The ethics letter warns that nurses may meet a suicidal or homicidal client who confides in no one else, and asks whether you are comfortable holding sensitive information. Comfort with confidential information never means promising secrecy about a threat to life. Telling the client that the nurse cannot keep the secret is honest but does not by itself protect the client. The first priority is the client’s safety: stay with the client and notify the provider and charge nurse so suicide precautions and a full assessment begin. Planning with family comes later, with the team.
questions.takeaway: Never promise secrecy about a suicide plan; stay with the client and notify the team at once.
questions.hintContent: What is the immediate risk, and who must know now?
questions.hintStrategy: For safety-versus-confidentiality items, choose the action that protects life now through the team.
questions.ref: Module 44 · Ethics · Values & Codes · Unit 7 slides 2–4; Ethics Letter to Students

questions.stem: Before her first clinical rotation, a nursing student answers the self-assessment questions in an ethics letter from her program. Which statements suggest she is ready to handle ethical dilemmas? Select all that apply.
options: “If I turn out to be wrong, I want to admit it and learn from it.”
“When a client asks what I would do, I can stay neutral instead of advising.”
“I’m willing to take a stand for a client when I believe I’m right.”
“I can accept both praise and constructive criticism from my instructor.”
“I usually change my opinion to match whoever pushes me the hardest.”
“I share interesting client stories with friends if I leave out the names.”
optionRationales: Correct. Willingness to admit mistakes and learn is a key self-check question.
Correct. Being able to stay neutral and avoid giving advice protects the client’s own decision.
Correct. Taking a firm advocacy stance on an issue you believe is right is part of ethical practice.
Correct. Accepting praise and constructive criticism shows readiness to grow.
Incorrect. Being easily swayed by outside pressure suggests values that are not firmly rooted.
Incorrect. This breaches confidentiality; clients can be identified even without names.
questions.rationale: The ethics letter asks students to take a critical look at themselves: identify their values and beliefs, notice whether they are easily swayed by pressure, be willing to advocate, admit being wrong, handle confidential information responsibly, stay neutral and avoid giving advice, and accept praise and criticism. These questions are a form of values clarification. Changing views under pressure and sharing client stories signal a need for more growth.
questions.takeaway: Know your values, advocate, admit errors, keep confidences, stay neutral, and accept feedback.
questions.hintContent: Recall the self-assessment questions about values, advocacy, confidentiality, and neutrality.
questions.hintStrategy: Select statements that show self-awareness and respect for the client; reject those showing pressure or privacy breaches.
questions.ref: Module 44 · Ethics · Values & Codes · Unit 7 slides 2–4; Ethics Letter to Students
